steps: Step 1, Look at a bean plant growing in a clear cup. Point to and name four parts: root under the soil, stem holding it up, green leaves on the stem, and a flower or bud at the top. Draw it and label each part.

Step 2, Say what each part does. The root drinks water from the soil, the stem carries water up to the leaves, and the leaves use sunlight to make food for the plant. Match each part to its job with a line.

Step 3, Test what plants need. Put two bean seedlings of the same size on a window sill. Water seedling A every day and give it light. Give seedling B no water for five days. Write what you see each day.

Step 4, After five days seedling A is still green and about 8 cm tall. Seedling B is dry, drooping and yellow. Conclusion: a plant needs water to stay healthy. Plants also need light, air and soil to grow well.

Step 5, Try a second case with light. Put one small potted plant in a sunny spot and one inside a dark cupboard for one week, watering both the same. The cupboard plant turns pale and weak, so light matters too.
Step 6, Your turn: name the four parts of a sunflower and say what a sunflower needs to grow. Answer: root, stem, leaf, flower; it needs water, sunlight, air and soil.

Step 1, Look at six animals: fish, cow, owl, frog, camel and lion. Make three groups by where they live: water, land and air. Fish and frog go in water, cow, camel and lion on land, owl in the air and trees.

Step 2, Sort by what they eat. Cow, camel and rabbit eat only plants, so they are herbivores. Lion and eagle eat other animals, so they are carnivores. Humans and bears eat both, so they are omnivores.

Step 3, Make a table with two columns: Animal and Food. Write cow, grass; lion, meat; hen, grains and insects. Count how many are herbivores. In our list of cow, camel, rabbit, lion and hen there are 3 herbivores, 1 carnivore and 1 omnivore.

Step 4, Explain with a body clue. A cow has flat teeth for grinding grass. A lion has sharp pointed teeth for tearing meat. A fish has fins and gills to live in water. Body parts fit where an animal lives and eats.
Step 5, Conclusion: animals can be grouped by home and by food, and their bodies help them live there. A camel lives in the desert and eats plants, so it goes in land and herbivore.

Step 6, Your turn: sort a duck, a tiger and a goat by home and food. Answer: duck lives in water and on land and is an omnivore; tiger lives on land and is a carnivore; goat lives on land and is a herbivore.
Step 1, Soak 6 bean seeds in water overnight. Next day, put 3 on damp cotton wool in a clear cup near a window and 3 on dry cotton wool. Label the cups Wet and Dry and write the start date.
Step 2, Check every day and record. Day 2, wet cup: seed swells. Day 4: a small white root comes out. Day 6: a shoot with two small leaves appears, about 3 cm tall. Dry cup: no change on any day.
Step 3, Conclusion from the test: a seed needs water to germinate. It also needs air and a suitable warmth. Light is not needed until the leaves grow, so many seeds sprout under the soil.

Step 4, Put the life cycle in order with numbers. 1 seed, 2 germination with root and shoot, 3 seedling, 4 grown plant with flowers, 5 fruit with new seeds. Draw arrows in a circle to show it repeats.
Step 5, Measure growth. A seedling is 3 cm on day 6 and 9 cm on day 14. It grew 9 - 3 = 6 cm in 8 days. Plot a simple bar chart with the two heights.
Step 6, Your turn: if a seed is planted in dry soil in a cold fridge, will it sprout, and why? Answer: no, because it has no water and not enough warmth.
Step 1, Match each animal to its habitat. Camel to desert, polar bear to snowy ice, fish to pond, monkey to forest tree, and cow to farm. Draw a line from each animal to a picture of its home.

Step 2, Explain one match using body clues. A camel has wide padded feet for sand and stores fat in its hump, so it can live in the hot dry desert. A polar bear has thick fur and fat to keep warm on ice.
Step 3, Match young to parents. A kitten belongs to a cat, a puppy to a dog, a calf to a cow, a chick to a hen, and a cub to a lion. Write each pair in a two-column table.
Step 4, Sort by how young are born. Hen, duck and frog lay eggs. Cat, dog and cow give birth to live babies and feed them milk. Count: of hen, cat, duck, cow, frog, 3 lay eggs and 2 give birth.

Step 5, Conclusion: animals live in habitats that give them food, water and shelter, and every young animal has a name that matches its parent. A fish out of water cannot breathe because it has gills.
Step 6, Your turn: match a duckling, a foal and a goat's kid to parents and say which hatches from an egg. Answer: duckling to duck, foal to horse, kid to goat; only the duckling hatches from an egg.
Step 1, Compare three soils: sandy, clay and loam. Put 100 mL of water on 100 g of each in a funnel with filter paper over a measuring cup. Time 2 minutes and measure the water collected.
Step 2, Record: sandy soil 80 mL, loam 50 mL, clay 20 mL. Sandy soil lets water pass fastest because its grains are big with large gaps. Clay holds water because its grains are tiny and packed tight.
Step 3, Work out how much water each soil kept: sandy 100 - 80 = 20 mL, loam 100 - 50 = 50 mL, clay 100 - 20 = 80 mL. Loam is best for most crops because it drains and holds a good amount.
Step 4, List ways water is used at home: drinking, cooking, washing, toilet, gardening. Tally a family day: bath bucket 20 L, cooking 10 L, drinking 5 L, washing clothes 40 L, total 75 L.
Step 5, Plan saving. Close the tap while brushing, which saves about 6 L. Collect rinse water for plants. If a leaking tap drips 1 L per hour, it wastes 24 L a day. Fix leaks to save water.
Step 6, Your turn: which soil is best for a pond lining and why, and how much is wasted in a week by the 1 L per hour leak? Answer: clay, since it holds water; 24 x 7 = 168 L.

Step 1, Compare three samples. A stone is a solid with fixed shape and volume. Water is a liquid with fixed volume that takes the shape of its container. Air in a balloon is a gas that fills the whole balloon.

Step 2, Pour 100 mL of water from a tall glass into a wide bowl. It still measures 100 mL, but the shape changed. A gas would spread out to fill the whole bowl. Record: solid keeps shape, liquid keeps volume, gas keeps neither.

Step 3, Show melting. Put 50 g of ice cubes in a cup at room temperature of about 25 C. After about 20 minutes it becomes 50 g of water. Mass stays the same because nothing is lost, only the state changes.

Step 4, Show boiling and condensing. Heat water in a pan with adult help until steam rises at about 100 C. Hold a cold plate above the steam. Water droplets form on it. This is condensation, gas to liquid.

Step 5, Write the changes: melting solid to liquid, freezing liquid to solid, evaporation liquid to gas, condensation gas to liquid. Heating drives melting and evaporation; cooling drives freezing and condensation.
Step 6, Your turn: what happens to a puddle at noon on a hot day, and which change is it? Answer: it dries up by evaporation, liquid water becoming water vapour gas.
Step 1, Stretch a rubber band over an open box and pluck it. You see it vibrate and hear a sound. Touch it lightly and the sound stops. Conclusion: sound is made when objects vibrate.

Step 2, Test pitch. Pluck a short thick band and a long thin band. The tighter, shorter band vibrates faster and gives a higher pitch. Pitch depends on how fast the vibration is: more vibrations per second means higher pitch.

Step 3, Test loudness. Hit a drum softly, then hard. The harder hit makes a bigger vibration and a louder sound. Loudness depends on the size of the vibration, measured in decibels, and has no link to pitch.

Step 4, Test travel. Tie a string between two paper cups and pull it tight. Speak into one cup while a friend listens to the other 5 m away. Sound travels along the string. It also travels through air, water and solids, but not through empty space.
Step 5, Record in a table: thin band, high pitch, soft; thick band, low pitch, soft; drum hard, loud. Conclusion: vibration makes sound, speed sets pitch, size sets loudness.
Step 6, Your turn: a guitar string is made shorter by pressing it. Is the pitch higher or lower? Answer: higher, because a shorter string vibrates faster.
Step 1, Gather one 1.5 V cell, a bulb, a switch and 3 wires. Connect cell, wire, bulb, wire, switch, wire back to the cell in one closed loop. Close the switch and the bulb lights.

Step 2, Draw the circuit with symbols: cell as two parallel lines, bulb as a circle with a cross, switch as a gap with a lever, wires as straight lines. Open the switch and the loop is broken, so the bulb goes out.

Step 3, Test objects by placing each in the gap of the circuit. Copper coin: bulb lights. Iron nail: lights. Rubber eraser: no light. Plastic spoon: no light. Wooden pencil body: no light. Pencil lead graphite: lights.
Step 4, Sort results. Conductors let current pass: copper, iron, graphite, aluminium foil. Insulators do not: rubber, plastic, wood, glass. Metals are generally good conductors.
Step 5, Explain safety. Never test with mains sockets. Use cells only. Wires are covered with plastic because plastic is an insulator, so it keeps current inside the metal and protects people.

Step 6, Your turn: a bulb does not light with a steel key in the gap, but lights with a spoon. What could be wrong with the key? Answer: it may be coated with plastic or paint that insulates, so scrape the coating and retest.

Step 1, Model day and night. In a dark room shine a torch on a ball with a sticker marking your town. Rotate the ball slowly anticlockwise. When the sticker faces the torch it is day, when it turns away it is night.

Step 2, Explain: Earth spins once on its axis every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day, the side facing away has night. The Sun does not move across the sky; the apparent movement is because of Earth's spin.

Step 3, Put sizes in order. The Sun is a star and is about 109 times wider than Earth. The Moon is smaller than Earth, about a quarter of its width. The Earth goes round the Sun once in about 365 days, one year.

Step 4, Observe the Moon. It does not make its own light; it reflects sunlight. The Moon goes round Earth in about 27 days. Draw the Sun, Earth and Moon in a row with labels and arrows showing orbit paths.
Step 5, Use a shadow stick. A 30 cm stick casts a long shadow of 50 cm at 8 am, a short 10 cm one at noon, and a long one at 4 pm. This shows the Sun's position in the sky changes through the day.
Step 6, Your turn: how long does one spin of Earth take, and what does one spin give us? Answer: 24 hours, which gives one day and one night.

Step 1, Take a hibiscus flower and label: petals (attract insects), sepals (protect the bud), stamen made of anther and filament (male, makes pollen), and pistil made of stigma, style and ovary (female). Draw and label.

Step 2, Describe pollination. A bee lands on the anther, pollen sticks to its body, and it carries pollen to the stigma of another flower. Pollen moves from anther to stigma: this is pollination. Wind carries pollen of grasses.

Step 3, Follow fertilisation. Pollen grows a tube down the style to the ovary and joins an ovule. The ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes the fruit. A mango's seed is inside the fruit made from the ovary.

Step 4, Seed dispersal matches seed design. Maple seeds have wings and spin in wind. Coconut floats on water. Burr seeds have hooks and cling to animal fur. Pea pods burst open and shoot seeds out. Make a table of seed, method and clue.

Step 5, Why dispersal matters: seeds that fall right under the parent plant compete for light and water. If a plant makes 200 seeds and only the 20 carried away find space, 10 per cent survive in new places.
Step 6, Your turn: a seed has a fluffy parachute like a dandelion. Say how it disperses and why. Answer: by wind, since the light fluffy hairs let it float far from the parent.

Step 1, Use a lever. A 1 m plank balances on a pivot at 50 cm. Put a 2 kg load 20 cm from the pivot. To balance it place a 1 kg weight at 40 cm on the other side, because 2 x 20 = 1 x 40. Load x distance equals effort x distance.

Step 2, Name the parts: pivot or fulcrum, load, effort. A see-saw has the pivot in the middle, a wheelbarrow has the load in the middle, and tweezers have the effort in the middle. Draw each with labels.

Step 3, Use a pulley. A single fixed pulley on a bar changes direction only: to lift a 1 kg bag you pull down with about 10 N force, the same as the weight, but pulling down is easier than lifting up.

Step 4, Gravity pulls objects toward Earth. A 1 kg mass weighs about 10 N on Earth. Drop a stone and a sheet of paper and the stone lands first because air resists the paper. Crumple the paper and both land almost together.
Step 5, Explain: a machine can make work easier by changing direction or force, but not by giving free energy. A longer lever arm needs less effort but a longer push distance.
Step 6, Your turn: a 3 kg load is 10 cm from the pivot. Where should a 1 kg effort be placed to balance? Answer: 3 x 10 = 30, so 30 cm from the pivot on the opposite side.
Step 1, Build a series circuit with two 1.5 V cells in a row (3 V total), two bulbs and a switch. Both bulbs glow equally. Unscrew one bulb and the other goes out because the loop is broken.

Step 2, Build a parallel circuit with the same cells, giving each bulb its own branch. Both glow brighter than in series. Unscrew one bulb and the other stays lit, which is why house lights are wired in parallel.

Step 3, Make an electromagnet. Wind 30 turns of insulated wire around an iron nail and connect it to a 3 V supply. It picks up 6 paper clips. Wind 60 turns and it picks up 12. More turns give a stronger magnet.
Step 4, Test a bar magnet on a tray of objects. It attracts iron nails, steel pins and nickel coins but not plastic, wood or aluminium foil. Two north poles repel; a north and south pole attract.
Step 5, Uses: electromagnets lift scrap metal in a yard and ring doorbells, and compasses use magnets to point north. A switch in the circuit turns an electromagnet off to drop its load.

Step 6, Your turn: if the nail picks up 6 clips with 30 turns, how many clips would you predict with 90 turns, and why? Answer: about 18, because more turns make a stronger field, assuming the same supply.

Step 1, Track moon phases for a month on a calendar. Week 1: thin crescent, then first quarter (half lit) on about day 7. Day 14 or 15: full moon. Day 22: last quarter. Day 29: new moon, almost not visible.

Step 2, Explain with a model. Light a lamp in a dark room and hold a ball at arm's length. Move it around your head. You see the lit part change shape because you view different amounts of the lit half. The cycle takes about 29.5 days.

Step 3, Order the planets from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The first four are rocky and the last four are giants. Jupiter is the largest. Use a mnemonic of your own to remember.
Step 4, Protect resources with numbers. A tap left running during brushing wastes about 6 L; for a family of 4 twice a day that is 4 x 2 x 6 = 48 L daily. Closing the tap saves 48 L, or 336 L a week.
Step 5, Other actions: reduce, reuse and recycle waste, switch off unused lights, plant trees, and use cloth bags. Each action lowers the use of water, energy or raw materials.
Step 6, Your turn: how many days from full moon to the next full moon, and what phase comes about 7 days after a new moon? Answer: about 29.5 days; first quarter.
Step 1, Make a mixture: 20 g of sand, 5 g of salt and 3 g of iron filings in a dish. Decide the order of separation by property: magnetic, solubility, particle size.
Step 2, Use a magnet wrapped in thin paper to pull out the iron filings. This is magnetic separation. Weigh the filings: 3 g, so all recovered.

Step 3, Add 100 mL of water and stir. Salt dissolves, sand does not. Filter through filter paper: sand stays on the paper as residue, salty water goes through as filtrate. Dry the sand and it weighs about 20 g.
Step 4, Heat the filtrate in an evaporating dish on a low flame until crystals of salt form. This is evaporation. It returns about 5 g of salt. Water vapour escapes, so only salt remains.

Step 5, Choose methods in general: handpicking for stones in rice, winnowing for husk and grain, sieving for flour and bran, sedimentation and decantation for muddy water, distillation for salt water into pure water.
Step 6, Your turn: how do you separate chalk powder from water, and ink colours? Answer: chalk by filtration; ink colours by chromatography on filter paper, since each dye moves at a different speed.
Step 1, Test candles and ice. Melt an ice cube in a cup at 25 C: it becomes water, the same substance, and can freeze again. This is a physical change, reversible, with no new substance.
Step 2, Burn a small piece of paper in a safe metal tray with adult help. It becomes ash and smoke and cannot return to paper. A new substance formed, so this is a chemical change.

Step 3, Add 1 teaspoon of baking soda to 50 mL of vinegar in a bottle. It fizzes and gives carbon dioxide gas. Bubbles and a new gas show a chemical change. Test by lowering a lit splinter: it goes out.

Step 4, Make a table with signs of chemical change: new colour, gas, heat or light, precipitate, new smell. Compare with physical changes: shape, size, state, no new substance. Dissolving salt in water is physical because evaporation brings the salt back.
Step 5, Classify: rusting of iron chemical, curdling of milk chemical, cutting a vegetable physical, boiling water physical, cooking an egg chemical, folding paper physical.
Step 6, Your turn: classify a rotting banana and crushing a can. Answer: rotting is chemical (new substances, smell, colour); crushing is physical (shape changes only).

Step 1, Draw a circuit diagram using symbols: cell as long and short parallel lines, bulb as a circle with a cross, switch as a break with a lever, and lines for wires. Draw a loop with one cell, one bulb and one switch.
Step 2, Draw two cells in series with the long line of one next to the short line of the other. Their voltages add: 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 V. A bulb rated 2.5 V glows brightly on 3 V.
Step 3, Test materials in a gap tester: copper wire, aluminium foil, steel spoon, graphite pencil lead glow the bulb (conductors); plastic ruler, rubber band, dry wood, glass do not (insulators).
Step 4, Record in a table with columns Material, Bulb glows, Type. Note that salt water also lights the bulb since dissolved salts carry charge, while pure dry sugar does not.
Step 5, Add safety: never touch a damaged wire, keep water away from mains sockets, and use only cells in class experiments. An insulator on a plug covers the metal to prevent shocks.
Step 6, Your turn: draw how a bulb, a battery and a switch connect, then say what happens to the lamp if the switch is open. Answer: the loop is broken so no current flows and the lamp is off.

Step 1, Test a bar magnet on 8 items. It picks up a nail, a paper clip, a steel pin and a nickel coin but not an aluminium can, plastic comb, or copper coin. Magnets attract magnetic materials: iron, nickel, cobalt.

Step 2, Find poles. Dip the bar in iron filings: most cling to the two ends, which are the poles. Hang the bar by a thread; it settles pointing north-south. The end pointing north is the north-seeking pole.
Step 3, Test attraction and repulsion. Bring two north poles together and they push apart. Bring north to south and they pull together. Like poles repel, unlike poles attract.

Step 4, Test air. Invert a glass over a floating cork in water; the water level inside stays lower, so air takes up space. Squeeze a closed balloon to show air can be compressed. Air also has about 21 per cent oxygen, which we need for breathing and burning.
Step 5, Test water. Measure 100 mL of water in a tall and a wide glass: the same volume takes different shapes. Water dissolves salt and sugar and is needed for all life.
Step 6, Your turn: which items in a pile of a rubber, a steel spoon, a coin of copper and an iron screw will a magnet lift? Answer: the steel spoon and the iron screw.

Step 1, Test a leaf for starch. Take a leaf from a plant kept in sun for 6 hours. Boil it in water, then warm it in alcohol to remove green colour, rinse, and add iodine. It turns blue-black, showing starch made by photosynthesis.

Step 2, Write the equation in words: carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, gives glucose + oxygen. Say where each enters: CO2 through stomata, water from roots, light absorbed by chlorophyll in chloroplasts.

Step 3, Control the test. A leaf covered with black paper for the same time stays brown with iodine, showing no starch. This proves light is needed. A variegated leaf stains only in its green part, proving chlorophyll is needed.

Step 4, Follow digestion of a cheese sandwich. Mouth: teeth chew and amylase in saliva starts breaking starch into sugar. Stomach: acid and pepsin digest protein. Small intestine: bile and enzymes finish digestion, and absorption goes into blood through villi.

Step 5, Trace the path: mouth, food pipe, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum. The small intestine is about 6 m long in an adult, giving a large surface for absorption. The large intestine absorbs water.
Step 6, Your turn: name the gas given off in photosynthesis and the organ where most absorption occurs. Answer: oxygen; the small intestine.

Step 1, Test conduction. Hold a metal spoon, a wooden spoon and a plastic spoon in a cup of hot water at 80 C for 2 minutes. The metal spoon handle gets warm quickly; the wood and plastic stay cool. Metals are good conductors of heat.
Step 2, Explain with insulators: air, wool, wood and plastic are poor conductors. Cooking pans have metal bases and plastic handles for this reason. Woollen clothes trap air and keep us warm.
Step 3, Convert temperature. The Celsius scale sets ice at 0 C and boiling water at 100 C. To convert to kelvin add 273: 37 C body temperature is 310 K. Fahrenheit is F = 1.8C + 32, so 37 C = 98.6 F.
Step 4, Use a laboratory thermometer. Place the bulb in hot water, wait until the mercury or alcohol stops rising, and read at eye level. Suppose it reads 60 C. Convert: 60 x 1.8 + 32 = 140 F.

Step 5, Link fibre to fabric. Wool comes from sheep, silk from cocoons, cotton from the cotton plant. The steps are fibre, spinning into yarn, then weaving or knitting into fabric. Wool is a good insulator.
Step 6, Your turn: convert 25 C to Fahrenheit and kelvin. Answer: 25 x 1.8 + 32 = 77 F; 25 + 273 = 298 K.

Step 1, Test rusting. Set up three test tubes each with a clean iron nail: A with water and air, B with boiled water covered by oil, C with dry calcium chloride and a stopper. After one week only A shows rust.
Step 2, Conclude: rusting needs both oxygen and water. Rust is hydrated iron oxide, Fe2O3 x H2O, a new substance, so it is a chemical change. Rust is flaky and weakens iron.
Step 3, Prevent rust by painting, oiling, galvanising (coating with zinc), or using stainless steel. Each method blocks air and water from the iron.

Step 4, Crystallise copper sulphate. Dissolve about 40 g of copper sulphate in 100 mL of hot water, filter, and let it cool slowly. Blue crystals with a regular shape appear in a day or two. Crystallisation is a physical separation from a saturated solution.
Step 5, Explain: a hot solution holds more dissolved solid than a cold one. On cooling, the extra cannot stay dissolved and forms crystals. Slow cooling gives bigger crystals.

Step 6, Your turn: a nail in dry air stays rust-free and a nail in salty water rusts faster. Explain. Answer: dry air has no water, so no rusting; salt speeds up rusting by helping the water carry charge.

Step 1, Show that air expands when heated. Put a balloon over the mouth of a bottle and place the bottle in a warm water bath at 60 C. The balloon inflates as air expands and becomes less dense, so it rises.

Step 2, Explain wind. Land near a coast heats faster in daytime. Warm air over land rises, creating low pressure. Cooler air from the sea, at higher pressure, flows in as a sea breeze. At night it reverses.

Step 3, Show air pressure. A glass full of water covered with card and inverted holds the card because air pressure pushing up on the card is larger than the weight of the water. Air presses on everything.

Step 4, Describe a cyclone. Warm ocean water, above about 26.5 C, evaporates and the rising moist air makes a low-pressure centre. Winds spiral inward at over 120 km per hour. The calm centre is the eye, with heavy clouds in the eyewall.
Step 5, Cyclone safety: listen to weather warnings, keep a torch, radio, dry food and drinking water, stay indoors away from windows, and move to a shelter if told to. Do not go near the sea.
Step 6, Your turn: air at one place is at 1000 hPa and at another is 1010 hPa. Which way does the wind blow? Answer: from the 1010 hPa place toward the 1000 hPa low-pressure place.
Step 1, Dig a small pit to see the soil profile. Layer A, topsoil, is dark with humus and roots. Layer B, subsoil, is lighter and has less humus. Layer C is weathered rock pieces. Below is bedrock.
Step 2, Test soil water holding. Pour 100 mL of water through 100 g of sandy soil and clay soil. Sand returns 80 mL, clay returns 25 mL. Retained water: sand 20 mL, clay 75 mL. Clay holds more water.

Step 3, Trace the water cycle: the Sun heats oceans, evaporation forms vapour, vapour rises and cools, condensation forms clouds, precipitation falls as rain, and runoff and infiltration return water to rivers and ground.
Step 4, Estimate saving. A 10 m by 8 m roof catches 80 m2 of rain. A 50 mm shower gives 80 x 0.05 = 4 m3 = 4000 L of rain. Rainwater harvesting can store part of that.

Step 5, Conserve water: use drip irrigation, fix leaks, reuse washing water for plants, and keep soil covered with mulch to cut evaporation. Planting trees reduces soil erosion and helps groundwater recharge.
Step 6, Your turn: a roof of 50 m2 gets 20 mm of rain. How much water falls on it? Answer: 50 x 0.020 = 1 m3, which is 1000 L.

Step 1, List the steps of growing wheat in order: preparing the soil by ploughing and levelling, sowing selected seeds, adding manure and fertiliser, irrigation, weeding, harvesting, threshing and winnowing, then storage.

Step 2, Calculate seed and yield. A field of 2 hectares needs 100 kg of seed per hectare, so 2 x 100 = 200 kg. If the yield is 4000 kg per hectare, the harvest is 2 x 4000 = 8000 kg, which is 40 times the seed.

Step 3, Compare manure and fertiliser. Manure is organic from decayed plants and animal waste and improves soil structure. Fertilisers like urea are manufactured, give nutrients quickly, but overuse pollutes water.
Step 4, Choose irrigation. Drip irrigation delivers water drop by drop at the roots and can cut water use by 30 to 50 per cent compared with flooding. Sprinklers suit uneven land and lawns.
Step 5, Explain storage. Grain must be dried to about 12 to 14 per cent moisture, kept in clean, dry bins, and protected from rats and insects, because damp grain grows fungi and spoils.
Step 6, Your turn: a 1.5 hectare field yields 3200 kg per hectare of rice. What is the harvest? Answer: 1.5 x 3200 = 4800 kg.
Step 1, Look at curd formation. Add 1 teaspoon of curd to 250 mL of warm milk at about 40 C and leave overnight. Lactobacillus bacteria turn milk sugar into lactic acid, so milk thickens into curd.

Step 2, Observe yeast. Mix 1 teaspoon of yeast and 1 teaspoon of sugar in 100 mL of warm water. After 30 minutes it froths with carbon dioxide from respiration. This makes dough rise in bread, and fermentation gives alcohol.

Step 3, List useful microbes: bacteria in curd and in vitamin and antibiotic production, yeast for bread and alcohol, bacteria in the soil that fix nitrogen, and bacteria that decompose waste. Penicillin comes from a mould.

Step 4, List harmful microbes and diseases: cholera and typhoid by contaminated water, malaria by Plasmodium through mosquitoes, tuberculosis through air, and fungi that spoil bread. Show a food chain from contamination to illness.

Step 5, Prevent spread: wash hands for 20 seconds with soap, boil or filter water, vaccinate, keep food covered and cold, and remove standing water where mosquitoes lay eggs. Refrigeration at about 4 C slows microbial growth.
Step 6, Your turn: explain why bread dough placed in a warm place rises faster than in the fridge. Answer: yeast respires faster at warm temperature, giving more carbon dioxide gas.

Step 1, Compare materials. Cotton and wool are natural fibres from plants and animals. Nylon, polyester and acrylic are synthetic fibres made from petrochemicals. Nylon is strong and light, so it is used in ropes and parachutes.

Step 2, Do a burn test on small safe samples held with tongs by an adult. Cotton burns with a paper smell and ash. Wool smells like burning hair. Nylon melts into a bead and shrinks away from the flame. Melting shows a synthetic.
Step 3, Compare in a table: absorbs water (cotton yes, polyester little), dries fast (polyester yes), strength (nylon high), cost and durability. Wash a 10 cm swatch of each and note wet weights.

Step 4, Explain plastics. They are polymers, long chains of repeating units. Thermoplastics like polythene soften on heating and can be remoulded. Thermosetting plastics like bakelite harden permanently and are used for electrical switches.

Step 5, Discuss environment: plastic is non-biodegradable and can last hundreds of years. Use the 5 R principle: reduce, reuse, recycle, recover and refuse. Sort plastics by recycling code and send to proper collection.

Step 6, Your turn: which fibre would you choose for a raincoat and which for summer wear, and why? Answer: a synthetic like nylon or polyester that repels water for the raincoat; cotton for summer as it absorbs sweat.

Step 1, Test properties of samples: iron, copper, aluminium, sulphur, carbon, and zinc. Metals are shiny, hard, malleable (hammer into sheets), ductile (draw into wire) and sonorous when struck. Sulphur is dull and brittle.

Step 2, Test conductivity with a 3 V circuit. Copper, aluminium and iron light the bulb. Sulphur does not. Graphite, a form of carbon, is a non-metal that conducts. Record exceptions: mercury is a liquid metal, graphite conducts.

Step 3, Test reactions with oxygen. Burn magnesium ribbon with tongs: bright white flame, forming magnesium oxide, a white powder that turns red litmus blue, so it is basic. Burn sulphur: sulphur dioxide dissolves to give an acid that turns blue litmus red.
Step 4, Write the equation: 2Mg + O2 gives 2MgO. Check atoms: 2 Mg and 2 O on each side. Conclusion: metal oxides are generally basic, non-metal oxides are generally acidic.

Step 5, Link uses to properties: copper for wires (ductile, conductor), aluminium foil for packing (malleable), iron for bridges (strong), sulphur for gunpowder and matches, carbon as graphite in pencils and as fuel.
Step 6, Your turn: a silvery solid hammers into a sheet and rings when struck. Is it a metal? Name its oxide's nature. Answer: yes, a metal; its oxide is likely basic.
Step 1, Identify the three needs of combustion: a fuel, oxygen from air, and heat to reach the ignition temperature. Remove any one and the fire stops. This is the fire triangle.

Step 2, Show it. Light a candle and cover with an inverted glass jar. The flame goes out after a few seconds when oxygen is used. Compare with two candles under jars of 250 mL and 1 L: the larger lasts longer.
Step 3, Compare fuels using calorific value. LPG gives about 55 kJ per g, wood about 17 kJ per g, and hydrogen about 150 kJ per g. Burning 100 g of LPG gives 100 x 55 = 5500 kJ.

Step 4, Draw the flame zones: inner dark zone with unburnt wax vapour, middle luminous zone with partial combustion, and the outer non-luminous zone with complete combustion, hottest part. A goldsmith uses the outer zone.

Step 5, Fire safety: water extinguishes wood and paper fires, but not oil or electric fires, where CO2 or foam extinguishers cut oxygen. Stop, drop and roll if clothes catch fire, and call the fire service.
Step 6, Your turn: how much heat comes from burning 200 g of wood at 17 kJ per g? Answer: 200 x 17 = 3400 kJ.
Step 1, Use P = F / A. A brick weighs 20 N. Its face areas are 0.02 m2 (large) and 0.005 m2 (small). On the large face: 20 / 0.02 = 1000 Pa. On the small face: 20 / 0.005 = 4000 Pa.
Step 2, Conclude: the same force on a smaller area gives more pressure. That is why a knife has a sharp edge and tractors have wide tyres. A pascal is one newton per square metre.

Step 3, Liquid pressure rises with depth. In a tall can with holes at 5 cm, 15 cm and 25 cm, water squirts farthest from the lowest hole. Pressure equals density x g x depth, so at 10 m in water it is 1000 x 10 x 10 = 100000 Pa extra.
Step 4, Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 101,000 Pa. It pushes on a 1 m2 surface with about 101,000 N, but our bodies push back with equal internal pressure.

Step 5, Friction opposes sliding. Pull a 2 kg block on wood with a spring balance: it reads 6 N. On a polished tile it reads 3 N. Rough surfaces have more friction. Rolling needs less force than sliding, so wheels help.
Step 6, Your turn: a 600 N person stands on two feet with total area 0.04 m2. Find the pressure. Answer: 600 / 0.04 = 15000 Pa.

Step 1, Apply the law of reflection. Shine a narrow beam on a plane mirror so the angle of incidence is 30 degrees measured from the normal. The reflected ray leaves at 30 degrees on the other side. Incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane.

Step 2, Describe the image in a plane mirror: virtual, upright, same size, laterally inverted, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. If you stand 2 m from the mirror, your image appears 4 m from you.
Step 3, Use two mirrors at 90 degrees. An object at the corner gives 3 images. The number formula n = 360 / angle - 1 gives 360/90 - 1 = 3. For a 60 degree angle it gives 5.

Step 4, Label the eye: cornea refracts light, pupil controls entry, iris adjusts its size, lens focuses, retina holds rods for dim light and cones for colour, optic nerve carries signals to the brain. In bright light the pupil shrinks.
Step 5, Link sound. Sound reflects as echoes. For an echo to be heard, the surface must be at least about 17 m away, since sound at 340 m/s takes 0.1 s for a round trip of 34 m.
Step 6, Your turn: a ray hits a mirror at 40 degrees to the normal. Give the reflected angle and the number of images with mirrors at 72 degrees. Answer: 40 degrees; 360/72 - 1 = 4 images.

Step 1, Test conductivity of liquids with a 6 V circuit and a bulb. Distilled water: no glow. Lemon juice, salt solution and copper sulphate solution: glow. Sugar solution: no glow. Ionic solutions conduct and give chemical effects.

Step 2, Electrolyse copper sulphate solution with two copper plates. The cathode gains a pink-brown coating. The anode loses mass. If the cathode gains 0.40 g and the anode loses 0.40 g, mass is conserved overall.

Step 3, Explain: copper ions Cu2+ move to the cathode and gain electrons, forming copper atoms that deposit. Copper atoms at the anode lose electrons and enter the solution as ions. The blue colour of the solution stays the same.

Step 4, Electroplate an iron key with copper. Make the key the cathode and a copper strip the anode in copper sulphate. After 20 minutes at a steady current it has a thin copper layer. Cleaned objects give an even coat.
Step 5, Name uses: chrome plating on taps, tin plating on food cans, silver plating on cutlery, and purifying copper. Plating protects against rust and improves look.

Step 6, Your turn: in plating a spoon with silver, which electrode is the spoon and which is the silver strip? Answer: the spoon is the cathode, the silver strip is the anode, in a silver salt solution.
Step 1, Use Newton's law of gravitation F = G m1 m2 / r^2 with G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2. For two 10 kg balls 0.5 m apart, F = 6.67e-11 x 10 x 10 / 0.25 = 2.67 x 10^-8 N, tiny.
Step 2, Find g on Earth. Using M = 6.0 x 10^24 kg and R = 6.4 x 10^6 m: g = GM/R^2 = 6.67e-11 x 6.0e24 / 4.1e13 = 9.77 m/s2, close to 9.8. Weight = m g, so a 50 kg student weighs 490 N.
Step 3, Compute work. A 20 kg box is lifted 3 m. Force needed equals weight 20 x 9.8 = 196 N. Work W = F x d = 196 x 3 = 588 J.
Step 4, Use energy. Potential energy at height is mgh = 588 J. If the box falls, KE at the ground is 588 J. Then v = sqrt(2KE/m) = sqrt(2 x 588 / 20) = sqrt(58.8) = 7.7 m/s, the same as sqrt(2gh).
Step 5, Power: lifting that 588 J in 4 s gives P = 588 / 4 = 147 W. Conclusion: work transfers energy; energy changes form but its total is conserved.
Step 6, Your turn: a 2 kg stone falls from rest through 5 m. Find KE gained and speed (g = 10). Answer: KE = 2 x 10 x 5 = 100 J; v = sqrt(2 x 100 / 2) = 10 m/s.

Step 1, Describe a sound wave. A tuning fork vibrates and compresses air then leaves a rarefaction, forming longitudinal waves. Mark compressions as high pressure and rarefactions as low pressure on a diagram.

Step 2, Define terms. Frequency f in hertz is vibrations per second, wavelength lambda is the distance between two compressions, and wave speed v = f x lambda. For f = 340 Hz and lambda = 1 m, v = 340 m/s.
Step 3, Solve for wavelength. Audible range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. At 340 m/s, a 20 Hz sound has lambda = 340 / 20 = 17 m and a 20,000 Hz sound has lambda = 340 / 20000 = 0.017 m.
Step 4, Do an echo calculation. A girl claps and hears the echo after 0.6 s. Sound speed 340 m/s means the total path is 340 x 0.6 = 204 m, so the wall is 204 / 2 = 102 m away.
Step 5, Link to uses: sonar sends ultrasound (above 20 kHz) and measures echo time, and ultrasound scans use frequencies of a few MHz. Loudness relates to amplitude, pitch to frequency.
Step 6, Your turn: a ship's sonar receives an echo after 4 s in water where sound speed is 1500 m/s. Find the depth. Answer: 1500 x 4 / 2 = 3000 m.

Step 1, Classify matter. Pure substances are elements like iron and compounds like water. Mixtures are homogeneous like salt solution or heterogeneous like soil and water. Test: a pure substance has a fixed melting point.
Step 2, Compare mixture and compound. Iron and sulphur mixed can be separated by a magnet. Heated together they form iron sulphide, a compound with different properties, not attracted by the magnet.
Step 3, Calculate mass percent. A solution contains 10 g of salt in 90 g of water. Solution mass = 100 g. Mass by mass percentage = 10 / 100 x 100 = 10 per cent.
Step 4, Calculate volume percent. 25 mL of alcohol in 100 mL of solution gives 25 per cent by volume. Mass by volume of 5 g in 200 mL is 5 / 200 x 100 = 2.5 per cent.
Step 5, Describe particles. States differ by spacing and motion. Evaporation occurs below boiling, and rate rises with temperature, surface area and wind. Convert 300 K to Celsius: 300 - 273 = 27 C.
Step 6, Your turn: find the concentration of a solution of 20 g sugar in 180 g water. Answer: 20 / 200 x 100 = 10 per cent by mass.

Step 1, Write symbols and valencies. Sodium Na is +1, chlorine Cl is -1, oxygen O is -2, calcium Ca is +2. Criss-cross: Na (1) and Cl (1) give NaCl. Ca (2) and Cl (1) give CaCl2. Al (3) and O (2) give Al2O3.
Step 2, Calculate molecular mass. Using atomic masses H = 1, C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40: H2O = 2 + 16 = 18 u. CO2 = 12 + 32 = 44 u. CaCO3 = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100 u.

Step 3, State the laws. Conservation of mass: in a reaction, 4 g of hydrogen forms water with 32 g of oxygen to give 36 g of water, so mass is unchanged. Constant proportion: in water H to O mass is always 1 to 8.

Step 4, Describe the atom. Sodium has 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 11 electrons, so atomic number 11 and mass number 23. Electron configuration is 2, 8, 1, with one valence electron that is easily lost.
Step 5, Compare isotopes: chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 have the same 17 protons but 18 and 20 neutrons. Average atomic mass about 35.5 u because of the abundance, roughly 3 to 1.
Step 6, Your turn: write the formula for magnesium chloride and its molecular mass (Mg 24, Cl 35.5). Answer: MgCl2; 24 + 71 = 95 u.

Step 1, Classify with the five kingdoms: Monera (bacteria), Protista (amoeba), Fungi (mushroom), Plantae (mango tree) and Animalia (tiger). Take the tiger: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Carnivora, Family Felidae, Genus Panthera, species tigris.

Step 2, Trace disease. Malaria is caused by Plasmodium protozoa spread by the female Anopheles mosquito. It is infectious. Diabetes is a non-infectious disease. Prevention for malaria: nets, drain standing water, prompt treatment.

Step 3, Explain vaccination. A weakened antigen trains the immune system to make antibodies and memory cells. A later exposure to the real pathogen is then met by a fast response. Herd immunity protects those not vaccinated.

Step 4, Follow the nitrogen cycle: atmospheric N2, nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium in legume root nodules, nitrates in soil, uptake by plants, passage to animals, decomposition to ammonia, and denitrification to N2.

Step 5, Follow the carbon cycle: plants take CO2 by photosynthesis, animals release it by respiration, and burning fossil fuels adds CO2. The greenhouse effect traps heat; rising CO2 warms the climate.
Step 6, Your turn: name the kingdom and one disease prevention for a mushroom and for cholera. Answer: Fungi; cholera is prevented by clean boiled water and sanitation.

Step 1, Balance iron plus steam: Fe + H2O gives Fe3O4 + H2. Fix Fe first with 3Fe. Fe3O4 has 4 oxygen, so use 4H2O. Then hydrogen gives 4H2. Final: 3Fe + 4H2O gives Fe3O4 + 4H2, with 3 Fe, 8 H and 4 O on each side.

Step 2, Balance aluminium and hydrochloric acid: Al + HCl gives AlCl3 + H2. Use 2Al to give 2AlCl3, which needs 6HCl and gives 3H2. Final: 2Al + 6HCl gives 2AlCl3 + 3H2. Check: 2 Al, 6 H, 6 Cl both sides.

Step 3, Classify. 2Mg + O2 gives 2MgO is combination and also oxidation. CaCO3 gives CaO + CO2 on heating is decomposition (thermal). Zn + CuSO4 gives ZnSO4 + Cu is displacement. AgNO3 + NaCl gives AgCl + NaNO3 is double displacement.

Step 4, Identify observations. The silver chloride in the last reaction is a white precipitate, so add (s) state symbols: AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) gives AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq). Zinc displaces copper because zinc is more reactive; blue solution fades.

Step 5, Identify oxidation and reduction in CuO + H2 gives Cu + H2O. CuO loses oxygen so it is reduced; H2 gains oxygen so it is oxidised. Together a redox reaction. Rancidity and corrosion are everyday oxidations.
Step 6, Your turn: balance Fe2O3 + CO gives Fe + CO2 and name the type. Answer: Fe2O3 + 3CO gives 2Fe + 3CO2; it is a redox reaction.

Step 1, Use the reactivity series K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Ag, Au. Predict: iron plus copper sulphate reacts (Fe is above Cu): Fe + CuSO4 gives FeSO4 + Cu. Copper plus zinc sulphate does not react.

Step 2, Explain ionic bonding in NaCl. Na (2,8,1) loses one electron to become Na+ (2,8); Cl (2,8,7) gains it to become Cl- (2,8,8). Opposite charges attract. Ionic solids have high melting points (801 C) and conduct when molten or dissolved.

Step 3, Explain covalent bonding in methane CH4. Carbon (2,4) shares one electron pair with each of four hydrogens, completing its octet. Covalent compounds have low melting points and are poor conductors.

Step 4, Name carbon compounds. Alkanes CnH2n+2: methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8. Alkene C2H4 is ethene with a double bond. Ethanol C2H5OH has an alcohol group. Ethanoic acid CH3COOH has a carboxylic acid group.

Step 5, Write reactions. Combustion: CH4 + 2O2 gives CO2 + 2H2O. Esterification: CH3COOH + C2H5OH with acid catalyst gives ethyl ethanoate, fruity smelling, + H2O. Saponification of oils with NaOH gives soap.
Step 6, Your turn: give the formula of the alkane with 5 carbons and say if Cu displaces Zn from ZnSO4. Answer: C5H12; no, copper is less reactive than zinc.
Step 1, Apply V = IR. A nichrome wire has a 6 V cell across it and a measured current of 0.3 A. R = V / I = 6 / 0.3 = 20 ohm. Doubling the voltage to 12 V gives 0.6 A, since resistance is constant.
Step 2, Combine resistors. Series 10 ohm and 20 ohm give 30 ohm. In parallel, 1/R = 1/10 + 1/20 = 3/20, so R = 6.67 ohm. With 6 V, series current is 0.2 A and parallel total current is 0.9 A.
Step 3, Use power and heat. P = V I. A heater at 220 V draws 5 A, so P = 1100 W. In 2 hours it uses 1.1 kW x 2 = 2.2 kWh. Joule heating H = I^2 R t.

Step 4, Describe magnetic effects. A current in a wire gives a circular field, found by the right-hand rule. A solenoid acts as a bar magnet. Force on a conductor follows Fleming's left-hand rule: thumb force, first finger field, second finger current.

Step 5, Explain the motor and generator. An electric motor turns a coil in a field using a split-ring commutator to reverse current every half turn. A generator turns a coil in a field to induce current by electromagnetic induction, shown by Fleming's right-hand rule.
Step 6, Your turn: a 40 ohm bulb is across 220 V. Find current and power. Answer: I = 220/40 = 5.5 A; P = 220 x 5.5 = 1210 W.

Step 1, Compare reproduction. Asexual: binary fission in amoeba, budding in yeast, fragmentation in Spirogyra, vegetative propagation by cuttings. Sexual reproduction involves two gametes and gives variation.

Step 2, Trace human reproduction: sperm from testes meet an egg in the fallopian tube, fertilisation forms a zygote that divides and implants in the uterus, the placenta supplies nutrients, and about 9 months later birth occurs.
Step 3, Do a monohybrid cross. Tall (T) is dominant over dwarf (t). Cross Tt x Tt: gametes T, t and T, t give TT, Tt, Tt, tt. Phenotype ratio 3 tall to 1 dwarf, genotype ratio 1:2:1.

Step 4, Do a dihybrid cross. Round yellow RRYY x wrinkled green rryy gives all RrYy. Selfing gives 9 round yellow, 3 round green, 3 wrinkled yellow, 1 wrinkled green. From 160 plants expect 90, 30, 30 and 10.

Step 5, Explain sex determination. Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes plus XX or XY. The egg always carries X. The sperm carries X or Y, so the child's sex is decided by the father's sperm with a 50 per cent chance each.
Step 6, Your turn: cross heterozygous tall Tt with dwarf tt and give the ratio. Answer: Tt, Tt, tt, tt, so 1 tall to 1 dwarf.

Step 1, Build a food chain. Grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, eagle. Name the producer (grass), primary consumer (grasshopper), secondary consumer (frog), tertiary consumer (snake) and top consumer (eagle). Add decomposers like bacteria.
Step 2, Apply the 10 per cent law. If grass captures 10,000 J, the grasshopper gets 1000 J, the frog 100 J, the snake 10 J and the eagle 1 J. Hence food chains are short, usually 3 to 5 levels.

Step 3, Analyse waste. Biodegradable waste like vegetable peels is broken down by microbes. Non-biodegradable waste like plastic stays. Biomagnification: a pesticide at 0.02 ppm in water can reach much higher levels in top predators.
Step 4, Discuss the ozone layer. UV breaks O2 and O3 in the stratosphere. Chlorofluorocarbons release chlorine atoms which destroy ozone, so their use was curbed. Ozone absorbs harmful UV.

Step 5, Plan resource use. Use the 3 Rs, rainwater harvesting, and water management. Compare coal and petroleum as non-renewable fossil fuels with solar and wind as renewable. Use CNG to cut air pollution.
Step 6, Your turn: a producer fixes 5000 J. How much reaches the tertiary consumer by the 10 per cent law? Answer: 5000 to 500 to 50 to 5 J, so 5 J.

Step 1, Follow the cell cycle: interphase (G1, S with DNA replication, G2) then M phase. In a 24 hour cycle, interphase takes about 23 hours and mitosis about 1 hour. A cell with 46 chromosomes copies its DNA in S phase.

Step 2, Describe mitosis: prophase (chromosomes condense), metaphase (align at the plate), anaphase (sister chromatids separate), telophase (nuclei form), and then cytokinesis. One 2n = 46 cell gives two cells with 46 chromosomes each.

Step 3, Describe meiosis. Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes with crossing over in prophase I, giving two cells with 23 chromosomes. Meiosis II separates chromatids, giving four haploid cells. Variation arises by crossing over and independent assortment.
Step 4, Count. Mitosis: 1 cell to 2 cells, DNA content 4C in G2 to 2C each. Meiosis: 1 cell to 4 cells, each with 1C. A human sperm cell has 23 chromosomes, and fertilisation restores 46.

Step 5, Cover biomolecules. Carbohydrates: glucose C6H12O6, starch, cellulose. Proteins: amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Lipids: glycerol and fatty acids. Nucleic acids: DNA with bases A, T, G, C. Enzymes lower activation energy.
Step 6, Your turn: a plant cell with 2n = 20 undergoes meiosis. How many chromosomes in each gamete cell and how many cells result? Answer: 10 chromosomes, 4 cells.
Step 1, Calculate moles. 5.85 g of NaCl has molar mass 58.5 g/mol. n = 5.85 / 58.5 = 0.1 mol. Particles = 0.1 x 6.022 x 10^23 = 6.022 x 10^22 formula units.

Step 2, Find a percentage composition. Water H2O is 18 g/mol, with H = 2/18 = 11.1 per cent and O = 16/18 = 88.9 per cent. Empirical formula from 40 per cent C, 6.7 per cent H, 53.3 per cent O: moles 3.33, 6.7, 3.33, ratio 1:2:1, so CH2O.

Step 3, Do stoichiometry. 2H2 + O2 gives 2H2O. 4 g of H2 is 2 mol and needs 1 mol of O2 (32 g), giving 2 mol of water (36 g). Limiting reagent: with 2 g H2 and 32 g O2, H2 limits and 18 g of water forms.
Step 4, Calculate molarity. 4 g of NaOH (40 g/mol) is 0.1 mol. In 250 mL, M = 0.1 / 0.250 = 0.4 mol/L.
Step 5, Assign quantum numbers for a 3p electron. n = 3, l = 1, m can be -1, 0, +1, and spin is +1/2 or -1/2. Maximum electrons in shell n is 2n^2, so n = 3 holds 18.
Step 6, Your turn: find moles in 11 g of CO2 (44 g/mol) and the number of molecules. Answer: 0.25 mol; 0.25 x 6.022e23 = 1.5 x 10^23 molecules.

Step 1, Predict trends across period 3: Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl. Atomic radius decreases because nuclear charge grows with the same shell. Ionisation enthalpy generally rises, with dips at Al and S. Electronegativity rises to Cl.
Step 2, Compare down group 1: Li, Na, K. Atomic radius increases, ionisation enthalpy falls, so reactivity with water rises. K reacts more violently than Na.

Step 3, Draw Lewis structures. For NH3, N has 5 valence electrons, forming 3 bonds with H and keeping 1 lone pair. VSEPR gives a trigonal pyramidal shape with HNH angle about 107 degrees. CH4 is tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees.

Step 4, Calculate bond order from molecular orbital theory. O2 has 12 valence electrons: 8 bonding, 4 antibonding, bond order (8 - 4)/2 = 2, and it is paramagnetic with 2 unpaired electrons. N2 has bond order 3.

Step 5, Compare electronegativity. HCl has a difference of 3.0 - 2.1 = 0.9, so it is polar covalent. NaCl has 3.0 - 0.9 = 2.1, so it is ionic. Hybridisation of carbon in ethene is sp2 and in ethyne sp.
Step 6, Your turn: give the shape and bond angle of H2O and the bond order of N2. Answer: bent with about 104.5 degrees; bond order 3.
Step 1, Use the ideal gas law PV = nRT. For 2 mol of gas at 300 K in 10 L: P = nRT/V = 2 x 0.0821 x 300 / 10 = 4.93 atm. Use R = 0.0821 L atm per mol per K.

Step 2, Use Boyle's law. A gas at 1 atm and 6 L is compressed at constant temperature to 2 L. P2 = P1 V1 / V2 = 1 x 6 / 2 = 3 atm. Charles's law: 300 K and 2 L heated to 450 K gives V = 2 x 450 / 300 = 3 L.
Step 3, Apply the first law, delta U = q + w. A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on the surroundings, so w = -200 J and delta U = 500 - 200 = +300 J.

Step 4, Calculate enthalpy. For CH4 + 2O2 gives CO2 + 2H2O(l), use formation enthalpies: CH4 -74.8, CO2 -393.5, H2O(l) -285.8 kJ/mol. delta H = [-393.5 + 2(-285.8)] - [-74.8] = -890.3 kJ/mol. Exothermic.
Step 5, Predict spontaneity with delta G = delta H - T delta S. For delta H = +40 kJ and delta S = +100 J/K at 500 K: delta G = 40000 - 500 x 100 = -10000 J, so it is spontaneous at 500 K.
Step 6, Your turn: find the volume of 1 mol of ideal gas at 273 K and 1 atm. Answer: V = 0.0821 x 273 / 1 = 22.4 L.

Step 1, Compare hydrogen isotopes: protium, deuterium and tritium with 0, 1 and 2 neutrons. Preparation in the lab: Zn + 2HCl gives ZnCl2 + H2. Industrially, CH4 + H2O at high temperature with nickel catalyst gives CO + 3H2.
Step 2, Compare s-block metals. Sodium reacts: 2Na + 2H2O gives 2NaOH + H2. Flame tests: sodium golden yellow, potassium lilac, calcium brick red, barium apple green. Reactivity rises down the group.
Step 3, Compare uses: sodium carbonate in glass and washing, sodium hydroxide in soap, calcium oxide (quicklime) in cement, calcium hydroxide in whitewash, and magnesium in alloys.

Step 4, Describe p-block. Boron forms borax; aluminium oxide Al2O3 is amphoteric; carbon exists as diamond (sp3) and graphite (sp2). Silica SiO2 is a giant covalent solid. Group 17 halogens oxidising power falls Cl > Br > I.

Step 5, Predict a reaction: Cl2 + 2KBr gives 2KCl + Br2, because chlorine is a stronger oxidiser than bromine. Ammonia is made by the Haber process N2 + 3H2 gives 2NH3 at about 450 C with iron catalyst.
Step 6, Your turn: write the reaction of calcium with water and the flame colour of calcium. Answer: Ca + 2H2O gives Ca(OH)2 + H2; brick red.
Step 1, Name by IUPAC. Choose the longest chain with the principal group. CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3: the longest chain has 4 carbons, with a methyl on carbon 2, so 2-methylbutane. CH3CH=CHCH3 is but-2-ene.
Step 2, Draw isomers of C4H10: butane (straight chain) and 2-methylpropane (branched). They are structural isomers with the same molecular formula and different structures. C5H12 has three isomers.
Step 3, Write substitution on alkanes. CH4 + Cl2 under UV gives CH3Cl + HCl by free radical chain steps: initiation, propagation, termination. Chlorine radicals form from Cl2 by UV.

Step 4, Write addition on alkenes. CH2=CH2 + Br2 gives CH2Br-CH2Br, decolourising bromine water (a test for unsaturation). Markovnikov: propene + HBr gives mainly 2-bromopropane because the more stable secondary carbocation forms.
Step 5, Write combustion and calculate: C2H4 + 3O2 gives 2CO2 + 2H2O. Ethene of 28 g (1 mol) needs 3 mol O2 (96 g) and gives 88 g CO2. Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution, not addition.
Step 6, Your turn: name the alkane CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH3 by the longest chain rule and write the main product of propene with HBr. Answer: 2-methylbutane; 2-bromopropane by Markovnikov addition.

Step 1, Identify pollutants. Air: CO from incomplete combustion, SO2 and NOx (acid rain), particulates. Water: nutrients causing eutrophication, heavy metals. Soil: pesticides. Name each with a source.
Step 2, Explain acid rain. SO2 + 1/2 O2 gives SO3 and SO3 + H2O gives H2SO4. Rain is acidic when its pH is below 5.6. Normal rain is about 5.6 because dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid.
Step 3, Explain the greenhouse effect. CO2, CH4 and N2O absorb infrared radiation re-emitted by Earth. A rise from about 280 ppm before industry to over 400 ppm raises mean temperature.
Step 4, Explain ozone depletion. In the stratosphere, CF2Cl2 gives Cl atoms under UV. Cl + O3 gives ClO + O2 and ClO + O gives Cl + O2. A single Cl can destroy many O3 molecules in a catalytic cycle.

Step 5, Use water quality numbers. Clean water has a BOD below about 5 ppm and heavily polluted water above 17 ppm, because microbes use dissolved oxygen to break down waste. Green chemistry principles: prevent waste, use safer solvents, high atom economy, and catalysis.
Step 6, Your turn: write the reaction that forms sulphuric acid from SO3 and say why rain at pH 4.5 is acidic. Answer: SO3 + H2O gives H2SO4; pH below 5.6 means extra strong acids dissolved.
Step 1, Calculate work with a force at an angle. A 50 N force at 60 degrees pulls a cart 4 m. W = F d cos 60 = 50 x 4 x 0.5 = 100 J.

Step 2, Use the work-energy theorem. A 2 kg block starts at 3 m/s and the net force of 4 N acts for 5 m. Work = 20 J. Initial KE = 0.5 x 2 x 9 = 9 J. Final KE = 29 J, so v = sqrt(2 x 29 / 2) = 5.39 m/s.
Step 3, Conserve mechanical energy. A pendulum bob of 0.5 kg is released from a height 0.8 m above its lowest point. mgh = 0.5 x 10 x 0.8 = 4 J. At the bottom v = sqrt(2 x 10 x 0.8) = 4 m/s.

Step 4, Conserve momentum in a collision. A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they stick. Momentum 6 kg m/s. v = 6 / 3 = 2 m/s. KE before 9 J, after 6 J, so 3 J is lost: inelastic.

Step 5, Compute power and centre of mass. A motor lifts 100 kg through 10 m in 20 s: P = mgh/t = 100 x 10 x 10 / 20 = 500 W. The centre of mass of masses 2 kg at x = 0 and 4 kg at x = 3 m is 12 / 6 = 2 m.
Step 6, Your turn: a 1 kg ball moving at 4 m/s hits and sticks to a 3 kg stationary ball. Find the final speed and KE lost. Answer: v = 4 / 4 = 1 m/s; KE lost = 8 - 2 = 6 J.

Step 1, Calculate stress and strain. A steel wire of length 2 m and cross-section 1 mm2 (1e-6 m2) carries a load of 100 N. Stress = 100 / 1e-6 = 1 x 10^8 Pa. With Young's modulus 2 x 10^11 Pa, strain = 5 x 10^-4. Extension = 5e-4 x 2 = 1 mm.
Step 2, Compute pressure in a fluid. In water at depth 5 m, gauge pressure = rho g h = 1000 x 10 x 5 = 5 x 10^4 Pa. With atmosphere 1.0 x 10^5 Pa, absolute pressure is 1.5 x 10^5 Pa.
Step 3, Use the continuity equation A1 v1 = A2 v2. Water in a pipe of 4 cm2 at 2 m/s narrows to 1 cm2. v2 = 4 x 2 / 1 = 8 m/s.

Step 4, Use Bernoulli's principle P + 0.5 rho v^2 + rho g h = constant. Horizontal pipe: v1 = 2 m/s, v2 = 8 m/s. Pressure drop = 0.5 x 1000 x (64 - 4) = 30000 Pa. Higher speed means lower pressure, as in an aerofoil.
Step 5, Surface tension and viscosity: capillary rise h = 2 T cos(theta) / (rho g r). With T = 0.072 N/m, r = 0.5 mm: h = 2 x 0.072 / (1000 x 10 x 0.0005) = 0.0288 m, about 2.9 cm.
Step 6, Your turn: find the speed in a 2 cm2 section if a 6 cm2 section has 1 m/s flow. Answer: v = 6 x 1 / 2 = 3 m/s.
Step 1, Apply the first law Q = delta U + W. A gas in a cylinder gets 800 J of heat and expands doing 300 J of work. delta U = 800 - 300 = 500 J, so its internal energy increases.
Step 2, Do an isothermal process. For 1 mol of ideal gas at 300 K, expanding from 2 L to 4 L, W = nRT ln(V2/V1) = 1 x 8.314 x 300 x 0.693 = 1729 J. delta U = 0 so Q = 1729 J.

Step 3, Use the second law and the Carnot engine. An engine runs between 600 K and 300 K. Efficiency = 1 - 300/600 = 50 per cent. If it takes 1000 J from the source it rejects 500 J and does 500 J of work.

Step 4, Kinetic theory: average KE per molecule = 3/2 k T. At 300 K, with k = 1.38e-23 J/K: 6.21 x 10^-21 J. The rms speed of nitrogen (M = 0.028 kg/mol) is sqrt(3RT/M) = sqrt(3 x 8.314 x 300 / 0.028) = 517 m/s.
Step 5, Use specific heats. For a monatomic gas Cv = 3/2 R = 12.47 J per mol per K and Cp = 5/2 R, ratio gamma 1.67. Heat 2 mol by 20 K at constant volume: Q = 2 x 12.47 x 20 = 499 J.
Step 6, Your turn: find the efficiency of a Carnot engine between 500 K and 400 K. Answer: 1 - 400/500 = 20 per cent.
Step 1, Describe SHM x = A sin(omega t) with A = 0.05 m and period T = 2 s. omega = 2 pi / T = 3.14 rad/s. Maximum speed = A omega = 0.157 m/s and maximum acceleration = A omega^2 = 0.49 m/s2.
Step 2, Spring-mass system. m = 0.5 kg and k = 200 N/m. T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k) = 2 pi sqrt(0.0025) = 2 pi x 0.05 = 0.314 s, so f = 3.18 Hz.
Step 3, Simple pendulum. L = 1 m gives T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) = 2 pi sqrt(1/9.8) = 2.01 s. Quadrupling L to 4 m doubles T to 4.02 s.
Step 4, Energy in SHM. For the spring system with A = 0.1 m: total energy = 0.5 k A^2 = 0.5 x 200 x 0.01 = 1 J. At x = 0.05 m, PE = 0.5 x 200 x 0.0025 = 0.25 J, so KE = 0.75 J.

Step 5, Wave speed v = f lambda. A wave of f = 50 Hz and lambda = 6.8 m travels at 340 m/s. On a string, v = sqrt(T/mu): with T = 100 N and mu = 0.01 kg/m, v = 100 m/s. Fundamental on 1 m string: f = v / 2L = 50 Hz.
Step 6, Your turn: find the period of a 0.25 m pendulum (g = 9.8). Answer: 2 pi sqrt(0.25/9.8) = 1.00 s.
Step 1, Calculate molality. 18 g of glucose (180 g/mol) is 0.1 mol, dissolved in 500 g of water. m = 0.1 / 0.5 = 0.2 mol/kg. Mole fraction of glucose = 0.1 / (0.1 + 27.8) = 0.0036.

Step 2, Find the boiling point elevation. delta Tb = Kb m = 0.52 x 0.2 = 0.104 K, so the solution boils at 100.104 C. Freezing point depression with Kf = 1.86: delta Tf = 0.372 K, freezing at -0.372 C.
Step 3, Calculate molar mass from osmotic pressure. A solution of 2 g solute in 1 L gives pi = 0.0246 atm at 300 K. M = wRT / (pi V) = 2 x 0.0821 x 300 / 0.0246 = 2002 g/mol, a polymer-like value.

Step 4, Apply the van't Hoff factor. 0.1 m NaCl has i near 2, so delta Tf = 2 x 1.86 x 0.1 = 0.372 K, twice that of glucose at 0.1 m. Relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the solute mole fraction.

Step 5, Calculate a cell potential. Zn + Cu2+ gives Zn2+ + Cu. E cell = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10 V. Nernst at 298 K: E = 1.10 - (0.0592/2) log([Zn2+]/[Cu2+]). With [Zn2+] = 1 and [Cu2+] = 0.01, E = 1.10 + 0.0592 = 1.159 V.
Step 6, Your turn: find delta Tf for 0.5 m glucose in water (Kf = 1.86). Answer: 1.86 x 0.5 = 0.93 K, so freezing at -0.93 C.

Step 1, Determine the rate law from data. For A + B gives products: expt 1 [A] 0.1, [B] 0.1, rate 2e-3; expt 2 [A] 0.2, [B] 0.1, rate 4e-3; expt 3 [A] 0.1, [B] 0.2, rate 8e-3. Doubling A doubles the rate, so order 1; doubling B quadruples it, order 2.
Step 2, Write rate = k [A][B]^2, overall order 3. Find k: 2e-3 = k x 0.1 x 0.01, so k = 2e-3 / 1e-3 = 2 L^2 mol^-2 s^-1.
Step 3, Use a first-order reaction. Rate constant k = 0.0693 min^-1. Half-life t1/2 = 0.693 / k = 10 min. After 30 min, [A] = [A]0 / 2^3 = 12.5 per cent of the start.

Step 4, Use the Arrhenius equation. Suppose the rate doubles for a 10 K rise from 300 K to 310 K. Then ln 2 = (Ea/R)(1/300 - 1/310) = (Ea/R)(1.075e-4), giving Ea = 0.693 x 8.314 / 1.075e-4 = 53.6 kJ/mol.

Step 5, Explain surface chemistry. Adsorption is physisorption (weak van der Waals) or chemisorption (bonds). Freundlich: x/m = k P^(1/n). Catalysts like Fe in the Haber process lower activation energy, and enzymes are specific biological catalysts.
Step 6, Your turn: a first-order reaction has k = 0.0231 min^-1. Find its half-life. Answer: 0.693 / 0.0231 = 30 min.

Step 1, Write electron configurations. Fe is [Ar] 3d6 4s2 and Fe3+ is [Ar] 3d5. Cu is [Ar] 3d10 4s1, an exception for stability. Transition metals show variable oxidation states since 3d and 4s energies are close.
Step 2, Calculate magnetic moment. Using mu = sqrt(n(n+2)) BM. Fe3+ with 5 unpaired electrons: sqrt(35) = 5.92 BM. Ti3+ with 1 unpaired: sqrt(3) = 1.73 BM. Zn2+ with 0 unpaired is diamagnetic.
Step 3, Study KMnO4. In acid, MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- gives Mn2+ + 4H2O. Oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+: 5Fe2+ + MnO4- + 8H+ gives 5Fe3+ + Mn2+ + 4H2O. 1 mol of MnO4- oxidises 5 mol of Fe2+.

Step 4, Name coordination compounds. [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 is hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride. Oxidation state of Co: x + 6(0) = +3 for the complex ion, so x = +3. The coordination number is 6 because six ligands donate electron pairs.

Step 5, Apply crystal field theory. In an octahedral complex d orbitals split into t2g and eg. [Fe(CN)6]4- is low spin (strong field) and diamagnetic; [FeF6]3- is high spin with 5 unpaired. Colour comes from d-d transitions.
Step 6, Your turn: find the oxidation state of Cr in K2Cr2O7. Answer: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0, so x = +6.
Step 1, Prepare haloalkanes. CH3CH2OH + SOCl2 gives CH3CH2Cl + SO2 + HCl, a clean method since the by-products are gases. Alternatively ROH + HCl with ZnCl2 (Lucas reagent) is used.

Step 2, Compare SN1 and SN2. A primary halide such as 1-bromobutane reacts with OH- by SN2, one concerted step with inversion and rate = k[RX][OH-]. Tert-butyl bromide reacts by SN1 through a carbocation, rate = k[RX], giving a racemic mix if chiral.

Step 3, Reactions of alcohols. Ethanol with acidified K2Cr2O7 gives ethanal then ethanoic acid. Dehydration with conc. H2SO4 at 443 K gives ethene; at 413 K it gives diethyl ether. Lucas test: tertiary alcohols turn cloudy at once, secondary after about 5 minutes, primary not at room temperature.

Step 4, Reactions of phenol. Phenol is acidic (pKa about 10) and reacts with NaOH to give sodium phenoxide. With bromine water it gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate. Reimer-Tiemann gives salicylaldehyde.
Step 5, Ether preparation by Williamson: C2H5ONa + CH3Cl gives C2H5OCH3 + NaCl. Use a primary alkyl halide, because a tertiary one gives elimination.

Step 6, Your turn: name the organic product when propan-2-ol is oxidised with acidified potassium dichromate, and say why it cannot oxidise further. Answer: propanone, a ketone, which has no hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon.

Step 1, Classify carbohydrates. Glucose is a reducing aldohexose giving C6H12O6; fructose is a ketohexose. Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose joined by a glycosidic link and is non-reducing. Starch is a polymer of alpha glucose; cellulose of beta glucose.

Step 2, Test: Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with glucose; Fehling's gives a red precipitate of Cu2O. Sucrose gives neither until hydrolysed with dilute acid to give glucose and fructose, called inversion.

Step 3, Proteins. Amino acids join by peptide bonds: glycine + alanine gives glycylalanine + H2O. Levels of structure: primary (sequence), secondary (alpha helix and beta sheet via hydrogen bonds), tertiary and quaternary. Denaturation changes shape, as when an egg is boiled.

Step 4, Nucleic acids: DNA has deoxyribose and bases A, T, G, C; RNA has ribose and U instead of T. A pairs with T by 2 hydrogen bonds, G pairs with C by 3. DNA of 20 per cent A has 20 per cent T and 30 per cent G and C each.

Step 5, Polymers. Addition: n CH2=CH2 gives polythene. Condensation: hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid gives nylon-6,6 with loss of water. Natural rubber is polyisoprene; vulcanisation with sulphur adds cross-links. Teflon comes from tetrafluoroethene.
Step 6, Your turn: a DNA sample has 30 per cent adenine. Give percentages of T, G and C. Answer: T 30, G 20, C 20 per cent.
Step 1, Apply Coulomb's law. Two charges of 2 microcoulomb each are 0.3 m apart in air. F = k q1 q2 / r^2 = 9e9 x 4e-12 / 0.09 = 0.4 N, repulsive.
Step 2, Find the electric field. A charge of 4 microcoulomb at 0.6 m produces E = kq/r^2 = 9e9 x 4e-6 / 0.36 = 1.0 x 10^5 N/C. The force on a 1 microcoulomb test charge there is 0.1 N.
Step 3, Calculate potential. V = kq/r = 9e9 x 4e-6 / 0.6 = 6.0 x 10^4 V. Work to bring 1 microcoulomb from infinity is qV = 0.06 J.

Step 4, Use Gauss's law for an infinite sheet with surface charge density sigma = 2 x 10^-6 C/m2: E = sigma / (2 epsilon0) = 2e-6 / (2 x 8.85e-12) = 1.13 x 10^5 N/C. For a sphere, flux = q / epsilon0 gives the same field as a point charge outside.

Step 5, Capacitors. A parallel plate capacitor with plate area 0.01 m2 and separation 1 mm has C = epsilon0 A / d = 8.85e-12 x 0.01 / 0.001 = 8.85e-11 F. At 100 V, energy = 0.5 C V^2 = 4.4e-7 J. A dipole has p = q x 2a.
Step 6, Your turn: find the field 0.3 m from a 3 microcoulomb point charge. Answer: 9e9 x 3e-6 / 0.09 = 3.0 x 10^5 N/C.

Step 1, Apply Kirchhoff's laws to a circuit. A 12 V battery with a 2 ohm series resistor feeds two parallel branches of 6 ohm and 3 ohm. Parallel resistance is 2 ohm, total 4 ohm. I = 12 / 4 = 3 A. Voltage across the parallel part is 3 x 2 = 6 V.
Step 2, Branch currents. 6 / 6 = 1 A and 6 / 3 = 2 A, which sum to 3 A, consistent with the junction rule. The loop rule: 12 - 3 x 2 - 6 = 0.

Step 3, Use a Wheatstone bridge. Balance condition P/Q = R/S. If P = 10, Q = 20 and R = 15, then S = 30 ohm. A potentiometer compares emfs by balance lengths: if E1 balances at 60 cm and E2 at 40 cm, E1/E2 = 1.5.

Step 4, Biot-Savart. A coil of 100 turns, radius 0.1 m, carrying 2 A has centre field B = mu0 N I / (2R) = 4e-7 pi x 100 x 2 / 0.2 = 1.26 x 10^-3 T. A long wire carrying 10 A gives B = mu0 I / (2 pi r) = 4e-5 T at 0.05 m.

Step 5, Force on a conductor and moving charge: F = B I L sin theta. 0.5 m of wire carrying 4 A in 0.2 T at 90 degrees feels 0.4 N. A proton at 10^6 m/s in 0.1 T moves in a circle of radius r = mv/(qB) = 1.67e-27 x 1e6 / (1.6e-19 x 0.1) = 0.104 m.
Step 6, Your turn: find B at 0.1 m from a straight wire carrying 5 A. Answer: 2e-7 x 5 / 0.1 = 1 x 10^-5 T.

Step 1, Use electromagnetic waves. c = f lambda. A 100 MHz FM wave has lambda = 3e8 / 1e8 = 3 m. Visible light of 500 nm has f = 6 x 10^14 Hz. Order: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma.

Step 2, Apply the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. A concave mirror has f = -10 cm and an object at u = -30 cm. 1/v = -1/10 + 1/30 = -2/30, so v = -15 cm, a real inverted image in front of the mirror, with magnification m = -v/u = -0.5.

Step 3, Use a lens. A convex lens of f = 20 cm with an object at 60 cm gives 1/v = 1/20 - 1/60 = 1/30, so v = 30 cm and m = v/u = -0.5, a real inverted image. Lens maker's formula 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2).

Step 4, Use Snell's law. Light going from air to glass n = 1.5 at 30 degrees: sin r = sin 30 / 1.5 = 0.333, so r = 19.5 degrees. Critical angle in glass is sin^-1(1/1.5) = 41.8 degrees, which allows total internal reflection.
Step 5, Young's double slit. d = 0.5 mm, D = 1 m, lambda = 600 nm. Fringe width = lambda D / d = 600e-9 x 1 / 0.5e-3 = 1.2 mm. Single slit first minimum at sin theta = lambda / a.
Step 6, Your turn: find the image distance for an object 40 cm from a convex lens of f = 10 cm. Answer: 1/v = 1/10 - 1/40 = 3/40, so v = 13.3 cm.

Step 1, Apply the photoelectric equation. Light of 400 nm has photon energy E = hc / lambda = 1240 eV nm / 400 nm = 3.10 eV. The metal work function is 2.3 eV. Maximum KE = 3.10 - 2.3 = 0.80 eV, so stopping potential is 0.80 V.

Step 2, Find the threshold wavelength for the same metal. lambda0 = 1240 / 2.3 = 539 nm. Light above 539 nm, like red at 700 nm, causes no emission, however intense, since each photon has too little energy.
Step 3, De Broglie wavelength. An electron accelerated through 100 V has lambda = 1.227 / sqrt(V) nm = 0.1227 nm. A 0.1 kg ball at 10 m/s has lambda = 6.63e-34 / 1 = 6.6 x 10^-34 m, not observable.
Step 4, Bohr model of hydrogen. E_n = -13.6 / n^2 eV. For n = 3 to n = 2: E = 13.6 (1/4 - 1/9) = 1.89 eV, giving lambda = 1240 / 1.89 = 656 nm, the red H-alpha line in the Balmer series.
Step 5, Compute orbit radius. r_n = 0.529 n^2 angstrom, so n = 2 gives 2.12 angstrom. Lyman series ends in n = 1, Balmer in n = 2. Shortest Lyman wavelength is 1240/13.6 = 91 nm.
Step 6, Your turn: find the photon energy of 200 nm light and say whether it ejects electrons from a metal with work function 4.5 eV. Answer: 1240/200 = 6.2 eV, which exceeds 4.5 eV, so yes.
Step 1, Describe the nucleus. Carbon-14 has Z = 6 and A = 14, so 8 neutrons. Nuclear radius R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 = 1.2 fm gives R = 1.2 x 14^(1/3) = 2.89 fm. Density is about 2.3 x 10^17 kg/m3.

Step 2, Calculate binding energy. Helium-4 has mass 4.0026 u against 2 protons (1.00728 u) and 2 neutrons (1.00866 u) sum 4.03188 u. Mass defect 0.0293 u x 931.5 MeV/u = 27.3 MeV, so about 6.8 MeV per nucleon.
Step 3, Radioactive decay. N = N0 (1/2)^(t/T). A sample with half-life 5 days is 800 mg. After 15 days, N = 800 / 8 = 100 mg. Decay constant lambda = 0.693 / T = 0.139 per day.

Step 4, Write nuclear reactions. Alpha decay: U-238 gives Th-234 + He-4. Beta decay: C-14 gives N-14 + electron + antineutrino. Fission: U-235 + n gives Ba-141 + Kr-92 + 3n + about 200 MeV. Fusion: 4 H gives He.

Step 5, Semiconductors. A p-n junction diode conducts in forward bias; in reverse bias there is a small leakage. A half-wave rectifier passes one half cycle. Silicon has a band gap of 1.1 eV. N-type doping with phosphorus; p-type with boron.
Step 6, Your turn: a 400 mg sample has half-life 2 h. How much remains after 6 h? Answer: 400 / 8 = 50 mg.
